history.heading: Taíno island and French colony
paragraphs: Haiti occupies the western third of the island of Hispaniola, which the Taíno called Ayiti, "land of high mountains". Columbus arrived in 1492, and within decades the Taíno population was almost wiped out by Spanish violence, forced labour and disease.

In 1697 Spain ceded the western part to France, which named it Saint-Domingue. It became the richest colony in the world, producing much of Europe's sugar and coffee, based on the brutal labour of hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans.

history.heading: The Haitian Revolution
paragraphs: In 1791 enslaved people rose up in a revolution led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines. They defeated French, Spanish and British forces, including an army sent by Napoleon. On 1 January 1804 Haiti declared independence, becoming the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people and the first independent country in Latin America and the Caribbean.
In 1825 France forced Haiti to pay a huge indemnity in exchange for recognition, a debt that burdened the country for over a century.

history.heading: Instability and dictatorship
paragraphs: The 19th and early 20th centuries brought frequent coups and political instability. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. François "Papa Doc" Duvalier ruled from 1957 and his son Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" until 1986, using the feared Tonton Macoute militia.

Jean-Bertrand Aristide, a former priest, was elected in 1990, overthrown in 1991, restored in 1994 and ousted again in 2004. A devastating earthquake in January 2010 killed an estimated 200,000 people or more and destroyed much of Port-au-Prince.

history.heading: Crisis
paragraphs: President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in July 2021. Since then, armed gangs have taken control of most of Port-au-Prince and spread into other regions, causing mass displacement and a humanitarian crisis. A Kenyan-led multinational security mission deployed in 2024, and in 2025 the UN authorised a larger Gang Suppression Force. No elections have been held since 2016.

culture.heading: Language and religion
paragraphs: Haitian Creole (Kreyòl) and French are the official languages; Creole is spoken by everyone, while French is used by a minority in education and administration. Most Haitians are Catholic or Protestant, and Vodou, a religion with African roots, is widely practised and officially recognised.
Haiti's revolutionary history is a source of deep pride, celebrated on Independence Day, when people traditionally eat soup joumou, a pumpkin soup recognised by UNESCO.

culture.heading: Arts
paragraphs: Haitian painting, with its vivid colours, gained international fame in the 20th century, and metal sculpture from recycled oil drums is distinctive. Music styles include kompa and rara. Writers include Jacques Roumain and Edwidge Danticat in the diaspora. Carnival and Rara festivals are major celebrations.

politics.heading: State in crisis
paragraphs: Haiti is formally a semi-presidential republic, but it has had no elected president or parliament since 2023. A Transitional Presidential Council was established in 2024 to govern and organise elections. State institutions are extremely weak, and armed gangs control large parts of the country.

economy.heading: The poorest country in the Americas
paragraphs: Haiti is the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere. Most people work in agriculture or the informal sector. Garment assembly is the main export industry, mainly to the United States, along with mangoes, coffee, essential oils (Haiti is a top producer of vetiver oil) and cocoa.

Remittances from the large diaspora in the US, Canada, France and the Dominican Republic are vital, amounting to around a fifth of GDP. Insecurity has caused food insecurity for millions. The currency is the gourde.
